name: Zoe Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 43, and lead the software team that matches care workers to visits for a tech company. I have a master's degree and know the scheduling rules, but what I like is fixing a shift that left someone unpaid; then I check with the client office that the wage was corrected. I use AI every day for draft tests, and my partner works as a school counsellor. We have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team the AI helper can draft schedule tests, but the care worker has to get the right paid hours at the end. I use AI every day and still check the actual rota before we release a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, I think my lead role and income hold. I earn a normal developer wage, my partner is a school counsellor with steady pay, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are several other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing the care-shift matching code and ask client offices about missed shifts. In the first year I'd keep AI on made-up worker records and save another 90 each payday while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household. A small tool is fine if it helps us find a worker who lost a shift in the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the passing test fail to count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A care worker called after the app moved her Tuesday visit to Wednesday and left her with an unpaid gap. The generated test passed because it checked the client's appointment, not the care worker's paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the extra savings transfer stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children know we write school costs into the budget before a holiday. If one wage changes, the extra savings transfer stops before we miss the mortgage.

say: I'd use **AI draft tests** only after checking care workers' paid hours.
I'd ask clients to report **unpaid gaps** as well as missed visits.
think: I expect **my lead role** to hold under modest AI change.
I have **four months saved**, two steady wages and some nearby software firms.
do: Keep checking **care-shift matching** against real rotas.
Use **AI sample records** for current tests, without real worker details.
Save another **90 each payday** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about income, focused on workers' lost shifts.
S0.quote: The generated test passed because it checked the client's appointment, not the care worker's paid hours.
fieldNote: **Two steady wages** and four months saved support calm under limited change.
She measures **worker pay**, not just client appointments, after a false passing test.

steps.text: Review care-shift matching code against actual worker rotas
Use AI draft tests only on made-up worker records
Save another 90 each payday while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can code, plan shifts and answer care offices, so we need to ask whose wages get lost when software makes a mistake. I would invite care workers into any tool review, not only our product managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be kept to sign releases, but the firm could shrink my team and then my hours. Four months saved helps, yet a mortgage and two children make a long income gap real; the care workers could lose money even sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a six-week check of AI shift suggestions against old rotas, counting unpaid gaps and staff time spent fixing them. If the trial cuts both, I'd learn the new approval method; during the first year I'd join our staff association in asking clients to share worker complaints before the firm changes headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own pay. A missing care shift can look like a tidy schedule and still take money from a worker. I can test the tool, but I need the people paid by the rota in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What failure belongs in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One care worker's missing Tuesday pay should count as a failure even if the client still got a visit. I'd show that case to the team before they set a speed target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be in the association discussion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association meeting would include developers, support agents and a care-worker representative from a client office if that office agrees. I'd ask for consent before using anyone's pay story.

say: I'd count **unpaid shifts** and the time staff spend correcting them, not just scheduling speed.
I'd invite **care-worker voices** into the rollout discussion with consent.
think: I could lose **my lead hours** as the team shrinks.
I fear care workers may lose **pay first** when AI misplaces shifts.
do: Check **AI shift suggestions** against old rotas for six weeks.
Learn **new approval methods** only if unpaid gaps and repair time fall.
Join the **staff association** to request worker complaints; invite a care representative only if the client agrees.
feel: **Anxious** about income and angry at hidden unpaid gaps.
S1.quote: A missing care shift can look like a tidy schedule and still take money from a worker.
fieldNote: **Planning and coding** are exposed, so her own hours may realistically shrink.
She demands **worker pay evidence** and client consent before bringing a care representative into staff discussion.

steps.text: Compare AI shift suggestions with old worker rotas for six weeks
Learn AI approval method only if unpaid gaps and correction time fall
Join staff association; invite client care representative only with client agreement and pay-story consent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 could make our code and shift planning cheap before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. Care workers still need a way to challenge a missing paid visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my team could be reduced sharply, including my lead job. Four months saved and my partner's counselling wage give us a short search, but the nearby firms might also stop hiring developers; my skill in today's system may not buy a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd map the mortgage and school bills with my partner and ask two care providers whether they have paid scheduling-audit posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real vacancies whose wage with my partner's pay covers mortgage and childcare; if none qualify, I'd use savings to search for other paid work and ask the lender about options before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can explain a lost shift, but explanation is not a wage when my own role ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real scheduling-audit job do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A provider's audit post would need authority to correct worker pay, not just send a report nobody reads. I'd ask for its written duties and hours before treating it as an answer to our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children after a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children that school stays the same while we check real offers. I would not tell them a promise from a phone call is a job.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches shift code before 2031 robots.
I'd ask for a **paid-shift appeal route** for workers.
think: I expect **my lead wage** could end quickly.
I have **four months saved**, but other developer vacancies may thin.
do: List **mortgage and childcare bills** now and ask two providers about paid audit posts.
After a cut, apply only to **real audit vacancies** with written duties and household wages covering bills.
If none qualify, search **other paid work** using savings and ask the lender before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the wage that supports our mortgage.
S2.quote: I can explain a lost shift, but explanation is not a wage when my own role ends.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** threatens coding and planning immediately; later robots are not a delay for her.
A replacement audit job needs **written authority** and combined wages that cover mortgage and childcare.

steps.text: Ask two care providers for written paid audit duties with pay-correction authority
Apply after cut to vacant paid audit posts if household wages cover mortgage and childcare
Search other paid work if no qualifying scheduling-audit vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives providers time to show who can correct a care worker's pay after a bad schedule. Robots follow around 2034 for hands-on care, but the thinking system reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep a paid role checking payroll effects if providers insist on it, though my software post could still shrink. I would rather prove the work is funded than collect a course certificate with no authority attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask one client to sign a small paid agreement for a monthly lost-shift audit, with worker consent and my employer's approval for the work. If it brings actual fees and fits around school pickup, I'd do one audit monthly while still employed; in the first year after 2031 I'd continue only while that client renews and the work pays enough to justify the time, then compare paid provider roles if my main job is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the main wage, but five years gives me room to test one service rather than buy a new career. I know a provider may say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the client actually buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The audit would count missing paid hours and show the provider which shift change caused them, with no worker names in a sample report. I would not bill a care provider before they signed the audit terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would school pickup fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner handles pickup on one afternoon now, but not every week. We would put the audit date on the calendar only after checking their school-counselling schedule.

I'd offer a **paid lost-shift audit** only with worker consent.
think: I might earn **client audit fees** if a provider pays and my employer permits it.
I could lose **my software wage** before that service grows.
do: Offer **one monthly paid audit** only after employer approval, client signature and worker consent.
Schedule it only if **school pickup** is covered and fees justify the time.
After 2031, continue only with **client renewal**; compare paid provider roles if my main post is cut.
feel: **Anxious** about the main wage, but able to test one paid service.
S3.quote: I would not bill a care provider before they signed the audit terms.
fieldNote: **Five years** let her test a tiny paid service without assuming clients will buy it.
The audit needs **employer approval** plus worker consent, client signature, school pickup and worthwhile fees.

steps.text: Offer one monthly lost-shift audit only with employer approval, signed client and worker consent
Schedule paid audit only if school pickup is covered and fees justify time
Continue monthly audit after 2031 only while client renews and fees justify time
Compare paid provider vacancies after 2031 if main developer job is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 lets us show what shift software does to a worker's actual pay. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, and hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a paying audit client or another developer job; I cannot assume either. Our wages and four-month cushion keep the next few years manageable, but I want the emergency account to grow before I promise a different career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing lost-shift bugs with care offices and add 90 from each payday to savings while both wages hold. If a provider signs and renews a paid audit with employer approval, worker consent and childcare arranged, I'd save the net fees after costs; in the first year after 2036 I'd change my main job only for a signed offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our present income, but attentive to what people still pay for. I would rather count signed fees than imagine a future market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe bug record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bug record would show the moved Tuesday visit and the missing wage without a worker's name. I want an employer to see the pay error we fixed, not someone's private rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you teach your children about apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask whether apps always know best. I tell them to ask who gains and who loses time or pay when a screen changes a plan.

I'd keep **lost wages** visible in product reviews.
think: I feel secure now with **two wages** and four months saved.
I cannot count on **future audit clients** without signed fees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both code and planning could cheapen before a worker can challenge lost pay. Clear notice, paid work with authority to fix wages and a way to contest bad schedules would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a correct visit means a correct wage. The client may see the right worker at the door while that worker loses a paid hour in the app; I want both checked.

headlineQuote: The client may see the right worker at the door while that worker loses a paid hour in the app; I want both checked.
portrait: Zoe, **43**, leads care-shift software development after a master's degree and checks whether scheduling bugs reduce workers' pay.
Her **typical pay**, partner's counselling wage, four-month cushion and some nearby firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **daily** but caught a passing test that missed a worker's unpaid gap.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about hours; fast 2028 AGI alarms her about job loss and wage errors.
With more time, she tests **one paid client audit** only with employer approval, worker consent, signed fees and school-pickup cover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead wage before paid roles exist to correct worker pay.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, paid pay-correction authority and a way to contest schedules would help.
